## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Chain steps together with the pipe `|>`.
2. Keep rows with `filter()` and columns with `select()`.
3. Sort rows with `arrange()`.
4. Add or change columns with `mutate()`.
5. Summarise data by group with `group_by()` and `summarise()`, and count rows with `count()`.

## Welcome to the tidyverse

On Day 4 you filtered rows with square brackets: `households[households$size > 4, ]`. It works, but it gets hard to read when you need several steps.

**dplyr** is a package of short, clearly named functions for working with data frames. It is part of the **tidyverse**, a set of packages that share the same style. Most R analysts use it every day.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

Every dplyr function works the same way:

- The first argument is a data frame.
- You refer to columns by name, without `$` or quotes.
- The result is a new data frame. The original does not change.

## The pipe: `|>`

The pipe takes the result on its left and passes it as the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as **"and then"**.

```{webr}
# Without the pipe: read from the inside out
head(arrange(penguins, body_mass_g), 3)

# With the pipe: read from top to bottom
penguins |>
  arrange(body_mass_g) |>
  head(3)
```

Both give the same result. The second version reads like a recipe: "take penguins, and then sort by body mass, and then show the first 3 rows".

::: {.callout-note}
## `|>` and `%>%`
You will see `%>%` in older code and online answers. It comes from the magrittr package and does almost the same job. `|>` is built into R (version 4.1 and later), so this course uses it.
:::

## `filter()`: keep rows

`filter()` keeps the rows where a condition is `TRUE`:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo")
```

Separate several conditions with commas. A comma means "and":

```{webr}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", island == "Dream", body_mass_g > 4000)
```

For "or", use `|`. To match one of several values, use `%in%`:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  filter(island %in% c("Biscoe", "Torgersen"))
```

Rows where the condition is `NA` are dropped. To find or drop missing values, use `is.na()`:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  nrow()
```

## `select()`: keep columns

```{webr}
penguins |>
  select(species, island, body_mass_g)
```

`select()` has helpers. A minus sign drops columns, and `starts_with()`, `ends_with()` and `contains()` pick columns by name:

```{webr}
penguins |> select(-year, -sex)
penguins |> select(species, ends_with("_mm"))
```

## `arrange()`: sort rows

`arrange()` sorts from smallest to largest. Wrap a column in `desc()` to sort from largest to smallest:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  arrange(desc(body_mass_g)) |>
  select(species, island, body_mass_g)
```

## `mutate()`: add or change columns

```{webr}
penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  select(species, body_mass_g, body_mass_kg)
```

You can create several columns at once, and later ones can use earlier ones:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm,
    long_bill  = bill_ratio > 2.5
  ) |>
  select(species, bill_ratio, long_bill)
```

## `summarise()` and `group_by()`: summarise by group

`summarise()` reduces a data frame to one row of summary values:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

On its own that is not much better than `mean()`. The power comes from `group_by()`, which splits the data into groups so that `summarise()` gives one row per group:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_mass  = max(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

`n()` counts the rows in each group. You can group by more than one column:

```{webr}
penguins |>
  group_by(species, island) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

`.groups = "drop"` removes the grouping from the result, so it does not affect later steps.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
`group_by()` plus `summarise()` does the job of a pivot table: rows are the groups, values are the summaries. The difference is that every step is written down, so you can rerun it on next month's data.
:::

### A shortcut: `count()`

`count()` groups and counts in one step:

```{webr}
penguins |> count(species)
penguins |> count(species, island, sort = TRUE)
```

## Putting it together

A real question: in the household survey, what is the average income of households **with water**, by district, from highest to lowest?

```{webr}
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")

hh |>
  filter(has_water == "yes") |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    households  = n(),
    mean_income = mean(monthly_income_ugx, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_income))
```

Each line does one thing, and you can read the whole analysis from top to bottom. To check your work, run the pipeline one line at a time: select the first lines and run them before adding the next step.

## Exercises

The `penguins` data and dplyr are loaded for every exercise.

### Exercise 1: Filter rows

Keep only the **Chinstrap** penguins that weigh **more than 3,800 g**. Save the result as `heavy_chinstrap`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_filter
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_filter
heavy_chinstrap <- penguins |>
  filter(______)
heavy_chinstrap
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
You need two conditions, separated by a comma: one on `species` and one on `body_mass_g`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
heavy_chinstrap <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap", body_mass_g > 3800)
heavy_chinstrap
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_filter
#| check: true
expected <- penguins[!is.na(penguins$body_mass_g) & penguins$species == "Chinstrap" & penguins$body_mass_g > 3800, ]
if (!exists("heavy_chinstrap") || !is.data.frame(heavy_chinstrap)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as heavy_chinstrap.")
} else if (nrow(heavy_chinstrap) == nrow(expected) && all(heavy_chinstrap$species == "Chinstrap") && all(heavy_chinstrap$body_mass_g > 3800)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: %d penguins.", nrow(expected)))
} else if (any(heavy_chinstrap$species != "Chinstrap")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Some rows are not Chinstrap penguins. Check the species condition.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = sprintf("You should get %d rows. Check the body mass condition: more than 3800.", nrow(expected)))
}
```

### Exercise 2: Select and sort

Show the `species`, `island` and `flipper_length_mm` columns, sorted from the **longest** flipper to the shortest. Save the result as `flippers`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_select
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_select
flippers <- penguins |>
  select(______) |>
  arrange(______)
flippers
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6_select"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
List the three column names inside `select()`. To sort from largest to smallest, wrap the column in `desc()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6_select"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
flippers <- penguins |>
  select(species, island, flipper_length_mm) |>
  arrange(desc(flipper_length_mm))
flippers
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_select
#| check: true
if (!exists("flippers") || !is.data.frame(flippers)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as flippers.")
} else if (!identical(names(flippers), c("species", "island", "flipper_length_mm"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Select exactly these columns, in this order: species, island, flipper_length_mm.")
} else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(flippers$flipper_length_mm[1], max(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The longest flipper should be first. Use desc() inside arrange().")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. The longest flipper is 231 mm.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Add a column

Add a column called `flipper_cm` with the flipper length in centimetres (divide millimetres by 10). Save the result as `penguins_cm`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_mutate
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_mutate
penguins_cm <- penguins |>
  mutate(______)
penguins_cm |> select(species, flipper_length_mm, flipper_cm)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6_mutate"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Inside `mutate()`, write the new column name, `=`, then the calculation: `flipper_cm = ______`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6_mutate"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
penguins_cm <- penguins |>
  mutate(flipper_cm = flipper_length_mm / 10)
penguins_cm |> select(species, flipper_length_mm, flipper_cm)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_mutate
#| check: true
if (!exists("penguins_cm") || !"flipper_cm" %in% names(penguins_cm)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "penguins_cm needs a new column called flipper_cm.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(penguins_cm$flipper_cm, penguins$flipper_length_mm / 10))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "flipper_cm should be flipper_length_mm divided by 10.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Summarise by group

Using the household survey, calculate the **median household size** for each district. Name the summary column `median_size`, and save the result as `size_by_district`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_summarise
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_summarise
size_by_district <- hh |>
  group_by(______) |>
  summarise(median_size = ______)
size_by_district
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6_summarise"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Group by `district`, then use `median(household_size)` inside `summarise()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6_summarise"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
size_by_district <- hh |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(median_size = median(household_size))
size_by_district
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_summarise
#| check: true
expected <- tapply(hh$household_size, hh$district, median)
if (!exists("size_by_district") || !is.data.frame(size_by_district)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as size_by_district.")
} else if (!all(c("district", "median_size") %in% names(size_by_district))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The result needs a district column and a median_size column.")
} else if (nrow(size_by_district) != 4) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get one row per district (4 rows). Did you use group_by(district)?")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(size_by_district$median_size[order(size_by_district$district)], as.vector(expected[sort(names(expected))])))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use median(household_size) inside summarise().")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Count

How many households grow each main crop? Use `count()`, sort the result from most to least common, and save it as `crop_counts`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_count
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_count
crop_counts <- hh |>
  count(______)
crop_counts
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex6_count"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Put the column name inside `count()`, then add `sort = TRUE`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex6_count"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
crop_counts <- hh |>
  count(main_crop, sort = TRUE)
crop_counts
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6_count
#| check: true
expected <- sort(table(hh$main_crop), decreasing = TRUE)
if (!exists("crop_counts") || !all(c("main_crop", "n") %in% names(crop_counts))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use count(main_crop, ...) and save the result as crop_counts.")
} else if (!identical(as.integer(crop_counts$n), as.integer(sort(crop_counts$n, decreasing = TRUE)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The counts are right. Add sort = TRUE so the most common crop comes first.")
} else if (identical(as.integer(crop_counts$n), as.integer(expected))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct. The most common crop is %s.", crop_counts$main_crop[1]))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Count the main_crop column.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using `=` in `filter()`.** Write `filter(species == "Gentoo")`, with two equals signs.
- **Forgetting to save the result.** `penguins |> filter(...)` prints the result but does not change `penguins`. Assign it: `gentoo <- penguins |> filter(...)`.
- **Quoting column names.** `select("species")` works, but `filter("species" == "Gentoo")` compares two pieces of text and keeps no rows. Write column names without quotes.
- **Forgetting `na.rm = TRUE` in `summarise()`.** One missing value makes the group's mean `NA`.
- **Leaving data grouped.** A grouped data frame affects later `mutate()` and `summarise()` steps. Use `.groups = "drop"` or `ungroup()`.

## Summary

- The pipe `|>` passes a result into the next function. Read it as "and then".
- `filter()` keeps rows, `select()` keeps columns and `arrange()` sorts.
- `mutate()` adds or changes columns.
- `group_by()` plus `summarise()` gives one row per group. `n()` counts rows in each group.
- `count()` is a shortcut for grouping and counting.
